speaker: Emily Heyward
title: EMILY HEYWARD: Build A Brand People Love (The Red Antler Way)
question: In B2B software and other technical industries, why does brand strategy matter even when buyers evaluate products functionally?
guest: I actually think it's even more important in the boring industries. A lot of times I'll have people ask me, "This is all well and good for consumer brands, but my business is B2B, and this isn't relevant to me." And my response there is, first of all, there's no such thing as B2B in that any product you're selling, any software you're selling, there's still a human on the other end who needs to make the decision. You still have competition, and often that human actually has to get buy-in from other people. So there's very rarely a solo decision-maker. If you're not providing that person first with a great reason why they should choose you, and then with the tools to get buy-in across the rest of their organization, you're relying very heavily on your product just speaking for itself. And these days that's less and less likely. Chances are there's another business that, if not doing the exact same thing as you, is taking more credit for the ultimate problem that you're solving. And it's very hard to stand out and to convince someone without thinking through how to convey your message in a succinct and powerful way.

points.core: B2B purchases rarely involve a single solo decision-maker inside an organization.

points.core: Relying on product quality alone lets better-positioned competitors claim credit for solving the problem.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Brand strategy matters in B2B because functional evaluation only happens among the vendors that make the shortlist, and brand largely determines who gets on it. Most buyers begin with a small set of vendors they already know, and research from Bain and others suggests the eventual winner usually comes from that initial set. At any given time, the vast majority of potential buyers are not in the market (the LinkedIn B2B Institute's "95-5 rule"), so being remembered when a need arises is worth more than being found during an active search.

Brand also reduces perceived risk. B2B purchases are high-stakes, made by committees, and hard to verify in advance; buyers cannot fully test reliability, support quality, or a vendor's longevity. A trusted brand acts as a proxy for those unobservable qualities and gives the decision-maker personal cover ("nobody gets fired for buying IBM").

Finally, features converge and get copied quickly, so functional parity is common. Brand then breaks ties, helps build consensus among non-technical stakeholders, supports premium pricing, and lowers customer acquisition and hiring costs.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Even in highly technical markets, functional evaluation does not happen in a vacuum—brand strategy determines which vendors get evaluated at all. Most B2B buyers enter a purchasing cycle with a shortlist of familiar vendors already in mind and overwhelmingly buy from that initial group, meaning unknown competitors lose before a single benchmark or proof of concept is run.

Once products are compared, rapid feature convergence makes purely functional differentiation fleeting, while critical qualities like future roadmap execution, support quality, and long-term vendor viability cannot be fully tested upfront. Because enterprise software involves steep switching costs and integration risk, buyers also face personal career risk if a deployment fails; a strong brand acts as a trusted heuristic that reduces perceived risk and breaks ties between functionally similar options. Finally, technical evaluators rarely buy alone. Closing a deal requires consensus from finance, security, procurement, and executive stakeholders who cannot audit code or architecture directly, and instead rely on brand reputation to validate the choice and justify price premiums.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Brand matters in B2B because a lot of the decision is made before any formal functional evaluation starts. Research from the LinkedIn B2B Institute suggests only about 5% of buyers are in the market at any given time. Studies from firms such as 6sense and Bain report that most buyers already favor a vendor when they first make contact, and usually buy from their initial shortlist. Brand largely decides who gets on that shortlist.

Buyers also judge risk, not just features. A purchase may involve a dozen stakeholders, cost a lot, and be hard to reverse. A trusted brand reduces the fear of choosing badly, which is the idea behind "nobody got fired for buying IBM." Google/CEB research found that B2B buyers feel strong personal stakes in these choices, often more than consumers do.

In crowded technical categories, competitors' features tend to converge. Brand then helps a vendor stand out, defend its prices, and avoid being treated as a commodity. A strong brand also makes sales cycles shorter, helps with hiring, supports partnerships, and encourages customers to stay and expand. Functional evaluation often ends up confirming a preference the brand helped create.
